lead: A beam-column is a member that carries axial compression and bending at the same time. The axial load acts on the already deflected shape, so it adds a moment of its own. The bending moment is therefore larger than the moment from the transverse load alone. Design uses an amplified moment, not the first-order one. Fuselage stringers under pressurisation bending and upper wing stringers, compressed by wing bending in flight and bent by the air load on their skin, are everyday aircraft examples. The same idea explains why a slender strut with a small side load can fail well below its Euler load.
prereq: You need beam deflection from Unit 2, the Euler load from Euler buckling of columns and end conditions, and the amplification idea from imperfections and eccentric loading.

sections.h3: Axial load on a deflected shape

blocks.text: A beam-column carries axial compression P and bending at the same time. The bending may come from a transverse load, from end moments, or from an eccentric line of action. If P were zero, the member would be an ordinary beam and the bending moment would be M(x), the first-order moment. With P present, the member deflects by v(x), and the axial force acts along a line that has moved sideways by v. The axial force therefore adds a moment P v at every section. That extra moment is not small near the Euler load.

blocks.where: E is Young's modulus, I is the second moment of area about the bending axis, v is the sideways deflection, x is distance along the member, P is axial compression, and M(x) is the first-order bending moment from transverse loads or end moments. The term P v is the extra moment caused by the axial load acting on the deflected shape.

blocks.text: The term P v couples axial load to deflection. You cannot find v from the transverse load alone and then add stresses, because v itself depends on P. The bending moment used for stress must include P v. A fuselage stringer under pressurisation bending also carries axial load from fuselage bending; an upper wing stringer is compressed by the upward bending of the wing in flight and bent by the air pressure on its skin panel. Both are beam-columns. A strut with an eccentric end load is the same problem, which is why imperfections and eccentric loading uses amplification.

sections.h3: Amplification for a simply supported member

blocks.text: Take a simply supported member of length L with axial compression P and a central transverse load W. The first-order mid-span moment is M<sub>0</sub> = W L/4. The Euler load of the same member is P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L². Suppose first that the first-order moment is itself sine-shaped, M(x) = M<sub>0</sub> sin(πx/L), as under a sine-distributed side load. Try v = v<sub>m</sub> sin(πx/L): substitution into the beam-column equation gives v<sub>m</sub> = M<sub>0</sub>/(P<sub>E</sub> − P) exactly. The total mid-span moment is M<sub>0</sub> plus P v<sub>m</sub>.
M<sub>max</sub> = M<sub>0</sub> + P M<sub>0</sub>/(P<sub>E</sub> − P) = M<sub>0</sub>/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>)
blocks.where: M<sub>max</sub> is the amplified mid-span moment, M<sub>0</sub> is the first-order moment, P is axial compression, and P<sub>E</sub> is the Euler load of the same member. The factor A = 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>) is the moment amplification.

blocks.text: At P = 0, A = 1. At P = 0.5P<sub>E</sub>, A = 2. As P tends to P<sub>E</sub>, A grows without limit. The figure plots A against P/P<sub>E</sub>; the worked example sits at P/P<sub>E</sub> = 0.603, where A = 2.52. The formula is exact for a sinusoidal first-order moment. For a central point load the exact factor is tan u/u with u = (π/2)√(P/PE): 1.82 at P = 0.5PE against 2.0 from 1/(1 − P/PE). The simple factor is about 10 % high there, so it is a safe estimate; an off-centre load or unequal end moments need a fuller analysis.

For equal end moments M<sub>0</sub> at both ends, the exact elastic result is the secant form M<sub>max</sub> = M<sub>0</sub> sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>)), where sec θ = 1/cos θ. This is the same secant that appears in eccentric struts. Use it when the first-order moment is constant along the member. For unequal end moments, a more detailed calculation or second-order computer analysis is needed.

The amplified moment is used inside a combined axial and bending check. A simple straight-line interaction is P/P<sub>cr</sub> + M/M<sub>u</sub> ≤ 1. P is axial compression, P<sub>cr</sub> is the compression capacity of the member (squash load or buckling load with the chosen factor), M is the amplified moment, and M<sub>u</sub> is the moment capacity about the bending axis. If the sum is below 1, the section is accepted by this check. Codes may use different exponents, but the principle is the same: the moment in the second term is the amplified one, not M<sub>0</sub>.

items: Compute P<sub>E</sub> with the correct effective length.
Compute M<sub>0</sub> from the transverse load or end moments.
Set M = A M<sub>0</sub> and use M in the interaction check.

blocks.text: For small P/P<sub>E</sub>, A is close to 1, and the axial load changes little. For P/P<sub>E</sub> above about 0.5, A is above 2, so a first-order check can be badly unconservative. On a fuselage, a stringer takes axial stress from overall fuselage bending and local bending from pressurisation; the interaction catches the combined effect. On a wing, an upper-surface stringer compressed by wing bending also bends under the local air load; the same check applies. Local buckling of the panel is a separate plate-buckling check.

figure.caption: Moment amplification against axial load. The simple factor 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>) (solid) and the exact factor for a central point load, tan u/u (dashed), both start at 1 and run away near the Euler load. The stringer of the worked example sits at P/P<sub>E</sub> = 0.603: 2.52 by the simple factor, 2.24 exactly.

spec.aria: Amplification factor against P over P E from 0 to 1. A flat dashed line at 1 for the first-order moment, a solid curve one over one minus P over P E rising steeply towards a vertical dashed line at 1, and a slightly lower dashed curve for the exact central-load factor. The worked example is marked at 0.603 with 2.52 on the solid curve and 2.24 on the dashed one.

examples.question: A simply supported aluminium stringer of length 1.0 m carries 15 kN of axial compression and a central side load W = 200 N, so the first-order mid-span moment is M0 = WL/4 = 50 N·m. E = 70 GPa, A = 250 mm², I = 3.6×10⁴ mm⁴ and c = 12 mm. Find the peak compressive stress at mid-span with the simple amplification factor, and compare with the exact factor for a central load.
steps: Euler load: P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L² = 9.8696 × 2520/1.0² = 24 871 N = 24.9 kN.
Bending stress: σb = Mmax c/I = 126.0 × 0.012/(3.6×10⁻⁸) = 42.0 MPa. Peak compression σ = 60.0 + 42.0 = 102.0 MPa.
Exact central-load factor: u = (π/2)√0.603 = 1.220 rad; tan u/u = 2.732/1.220 = 2.239. Mmax = 112.0 N·m, σb = 37.3 MPa, peak 97.3 MPa.
examples.answer: Peak compressive stress 102.0 MPa with the simple factor (97.3 MPa with the exact central-load factor). The first-order check, 60 + 16.7 = 76.7 MPa, would miss a quarter of it.

traps: Adding the axial stress and the first-order bending stress and stopping there. The axial load also increases the moment, and that amplified moment often controls the design.
Using P<sub>E</sub> for pinned ends when the real member has different end restraint. The effective length changes P<sub>E</sub>, and the amplification 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>) changes with it.
Mixing units in the bending stress: M in N m needs c in m and I in m⁴. A value of I in mm⁴ must be multiplied by 10⁻¹².

Applying 1/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>) to every transverse load or end moment. It is exact only for a sine-shaped first-order moment; it is close for a central load and approximate for other cases. Equal end moments need the secant form.
Using the formula above P = P<sub>E</sub>. The member has then buckled; the amplification is meaningless and a second-order or buckling analysis is required.

quiz.a: A member that carries axial compression and bending at the same time. The axial load acts on the deflected shape and adds an extra moment.

quiz.q: Why does axial compression increase the bending moment in a beam?
quiz.a: The axial force acts along a line displaced sideways by the deflection v, so it adds a moment P v. This extra moment increases deflection, which further increases the moment.

quiz.q: A simply supported member has P<sub>E</sub> = 30 kN, P = 12 kN and a transverse load giving M0 = 0.08 kN m. Find the amplified moment.
Why is Mmax = M0/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>) close for a central load but not exact for a load near one end?
quiz.a: The derivation assumes a sine-shaped first-order moment and deflection. A central load is close to that shape. A load near one end gives a different moment shape, so the amplification differs; a secant form or a numerical second-order solution is needed.

quiz.q: State the simple interaction check for a beam-column and define its terms.
quiz.a: P/Pcr + M/Mu ≤ 1, where P is axial compression, Pcr is compression capacity, M is the amplified moment, and Mu is moment capacity about the bending axis.

quiz.q: A member has equal end moments M0 = 2 kN m and P/P<sub>E</sub> = 0.36. Use the secant form to find Mmax.
What happens to the moment amplification as P approaches P<sub>E</sub>, and what does it mean for design?
quiz.a: The amplification tends to infinity. The member buckles at P<sub>E</sub>, and linear beam-column theory is not valid close to that load. Design keeps a margin below P<sub>E</sub> and uses the amplified moment in the interaction check.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real aircraft frames are analysed with second-order finite element models that include geometric stiffness, so the axial load stiffens or softens the bending stiffness directly. The same amplification appears in civil building frames as the P-Delta effect. Aerospace panels add local buckling and post-buckling, which the simple beam-column equation does not cover. Search for beam-column amplification, secant formula, geometric stiffness and P-Delta to go further.
